raw_response:
I am 52 years old, and I have worked this land since I was 22. My mother taught me how to farm, and I have never sat in a classroom, but I know my 20.8 mu better than anyone. My husband and son work in a factory in the city, so it is me and my daughter-in-law at home. We have a well, and I thank the heavens it still gives water, though I am careful with it because the groundwater is not what it used to be.

My wheat went in last October on all 20.8 mu, as it always does. I buy improved seed from the township station — it costs more than keeping my own, but the yield is better and I do not have to clean it. I rotary-till before planting to break the soil and bury the stubble. Now the wheat is waking up from winter. I will irrigate three times: once at green-up, once at jointing, and once at grain-filling. I split the nitrogen — half at green-up and half at jointing — because I learned long ago that putting it all down at once is wasteful. The phosphorus and potash were put down last autumn as basal dressing. I spray twice: herbicide in early spring, and insecticide if the aphids come, which they usually do.

After wheat harvest in early June, I do not rest. The maize must go in the same day if possible — we only have about 100 frost-free days. I plant hybrid maize seed, no-till straight into the wheat stubble. There is no time to plough, and the stubble keeps the moisture in the ground. Maize needs less fuss. I irrigate twice: once when it is knee-high, and once at silking. I spray twice: herbicide at the seedling stage, and insecticide for corn borer if I see it. I topdress urea when the plants are at the big-flush stage.

I do not chase crazy yields with bags of extra fertilizer like some of the younger farmers. I know my soil. I expect about 500 kg of wheat per mu and about 550 kg of maize per mu. That is enough to feed the family, sell a little, and pay for the inputs for next year.
